newsitem.title: USA: Variety of conditions awaits U.S. SRW wheat tour.
newsitem.headline: Variety of conditions awaits U.S. SRW wheat tour.

text.p: Participants in the U.S. soft red winter wheat tour are expected to see a wide range of crop conditions and yield prospects ranging from above to below average as they scout fields in key producing states next week.
"We are going to see some problems but we will see some of the best wheat in years in some places," said tour leader Jim Quinton, a Consolidated Grain and Barge grain merchandiser.
The tour, sponsored by the Wheat Quality Council, is scheduled to start on June 9 at Toledo, Ohio, sweeping through northwest Ohio, southeast Michigan and northeastern Indiana.
Subsequent days will take the tour through parts of Kentucky, Missouri and Arkansas.
About 60 participants from all segments of the grain industry will be scouting a high concentration of winter wheat acreage in the tri-state area on Monday, Quinton said.
But several crop experts noted a cool, wet spring has caused some disease problems and potential yield losses there.

"Our biggest problem is that we are right in the middle of heading and we are concerned about scab, a fungal disease that attacks the wheat heads in the developing kernel," said Pat Lipps, extension plant pathologist, Ohio State University.
Lipps, who is not a tour participant this year, warned more wet weather could cause scab infections and potential yield losses in some Ohio fields.
On June 10, participants will scout areas in southern Illinois, southwest Indiana and western Kentucky. Quinton said he expects that area to have the best yields and quality prospects.

But Indiana may have some disease concerns. "At least in certain varieties of wheat, we think there will be some yield losses as a result of viral infections," said Chuck Mansfield, Purdue University extension agronomist.
"We don't know yet what scab or glume blotch (a fungal head disease) will hold for us. It all depends on the weather until the harvest in late June," Mansfield said.

Mansfield said the wheat in southwestern Indiana was in the grain fill stage of development. "That means flowering and pollination have already occurred and the grains are filling. So this is a critical time for the plant," he said.
The tour will conclude on June 11 in Little Rock, Ark., after participants trek through fields in the boot heel of Missouri and eastern Arkansas.
"I'm expecting to find in the aftermath of a very wet, difficult winter, a greater amount of abandonment in Arkansas which may have reduced this year's production," Quinton said.

"Continued rains in Arkansas appeared to be causing a lot of harvest problems down there," said Don Mennel, president of Mennel Milling Company in Fostoria, Ohio and a participant in previous tours. "I think they are having trouble getting the crops out."
In its May report, the U.S. Department of Agriculture pegged the 1997 soft red winter wheat crop at 408.86 million bushels, which would be down from 422.02 million bushels in 1996.
Total 1996 U.S. wheat production was 2.28 billion bushels.
